words.lemma: clun (fem., here lenited after dual 'dwy': 'the two hips/haunches'; subject)

cognate: Welsh llydan ~ Av. pərəθu- ~ Skt pṛthu- (all *pl̥th₂-, 'broad'); Welsh clun ~ Av. sraoni- ~ Skt śroṇi- (all *ḱlowni-, 'hip, haunch'); both members cognate in each branch
drift_or_renewal: different stem formation of the adjective (Brittonic *-no- vs Indo-Iranian *-u-); Indo-Iranian fuses the pair into a bahuvrihi compound, Welsh keeps it analytic (predicate adjective)
shared_syntax: adjective 'broad' qualifying 'hip(s)' as one feature in a body description; compound epithet in Avestan (and Sanskrit), predicative 'the two hips were broad' in Welsh
context: Both are head-to-foot catalogues of the body of a supernatural figure: Yt 15.54 lists Vayu's bodily epithets (bərəzi.pāδō, pərəθu.varō 'broad-breasted', pərəθu.sraoniš); Peredur's description of the black Loathly Damsel runs face, nose, eyes, teeth, belly, breasts, back, then 'y dwy glun oed yn llydan ... ac yn vein oll o hynny y waeret' (thin below), then feet and knees. Epic Sanskrit uses pṛthuśroṇī as a vocative epithet of beautiful women. The Welsh catalogue is a grotesque inversion of a beauty description, which fits a formerly positive epithet turned to an ugly feature (broad and bony). Caveat: Indo-Iranian compound is an exact Avestan-Sanskrit match; the Welsh witness is analytic and 'broad hips' is a natural description, so chance is high. Welsh 'ŷfcỳanic' after llydan is an OCR-damaged adjective, probably ysgyrnig 'bony'. Middle Welsh prose, late.

note: Slab dominated by Irish annal entries (Annals of Ulster / Four Masters obits and raids) with unrelated Greek prose partners; one low claim. Considered and rejected: 'great snow and frost' pairing (Ir. snechta/reód, sioc in many annal entries; ON Gylfaginning sníor/frost; OE Azarias forst and sniw; Lat. nix/pruina, OHG snêuue/irfróren; BC-28370, BC-cd646, BC-7bb9c, BC-f0288) as generic weather vocabulary; Ir. 'lán Éire do chlú' (BC-991d4, BC-f828b) vs Gk κλέος partner without congruent syntax.
